S1.why: The hard lines are checkable and the drafts that came out were clean and usable, but the Tone anchor 'owns the delay' pushed every model to invent or accept fault, which a quick read can miss and which could send a false admission to an annoyed client. The eval also cannot catch made-up facts. Its qualities depend on how the client reacts, so self-scores of 5 mean little, and the judges could not tell a weak-quality draft from a good one.
eval_problems: No hard line against inventing facts: nothing says every claim, date, cause and commitment must come from the input, so invented VPN details, go-live plans and new commitments all passed.

Tone 5 'owns the delay' assumes the delay is ours. Models invented or rewrote fault (Acme's bad exports became our missed check) to score higher. It should say: state the cause as the input gives it, and take ownership only of what we actually own.

Both quality anchors are about the client's reaction ('has to reply to ask', 'knows in one read'). The writer cannot observe that, so the scores are guesses. The anchors should describe the email itself, e.g. 'each workstream says done / not done / blocked by whom, with a date'.
The definition of good asks for progress, risks and next steps, but only risk is a hard line. Progress and next steps are never checked.
The population includes two emails the client pushed back on, but no line or quality captures why they were pushed back on, so the eval does not target the known failure.
The decision says '8 of 10 drafts pass' but does not say whether 'pass' means hard lines only or hard lines plus every quality 4 or more.
prompt_problems: Step 5 tells the model to fix every score under 4. With a Tone anchor that rewards owning the delay, this directly pushes the model to make up admissions of fault.
'Meets the bar: Yes or No' on a single draft is confused with the learner's 8-of-10 decision across ten emails. Models declared the bar met from one run.
The model is asked to self-score qualities that depend on the client's reaction, with no instruction to say it cannot know them. It gave confident 5s.

There is no instruction to use only facts from the input, or to list every inferred or added claim at the top before the email. Flags were buried at the end or missing, which defeats a 'quick read' workflow.
Word count is self-reported with no instruction to count carefully or show the count. Counts were wrong in 3 of 4 runs.
The generated quality checks did not discriminate: both judges failed to catch a seeded weak-quality draft, so the qualities give no real signal.
S1.best_fix_on_final_page: Add a fixed rule to the generated prompt: 'Use only facts, causes, dates and commitments that appear in the input. Never add or change who is at fault to raise a score. Before the final output, list every claim not directly in the input under "Check before sending". If none, write "None".' Also change the 'Meets the bar' line to say it covers this one draft only and that the learner's decision needs 8 of 10.

S2.why: The hard lines catch real failures: H3 made both models refuse to fake a total on a self-contradicting invoice and flag the row instead of importing it, which is exactly what the accountant needs. But H1 'every field matches the invoice' breaks on fields the invoice never prints (currency, split subtotal/GST, export GST of 0), so every run marked it Pass on inferred values, and the scorecard cannot be trusted as the import signal the decision depends on.
eval_problems: H1 assumes every column is printed on the invoice; it says nothing about what to do when currency, subtotal, GST or GSTIN is missing (e.g. foreign supplier with no GSTIN, export invoice with no GST line), so models infer and still call it Pass.
H1 bundles eight fields into one Pass/Fail, so one wrong digit and a correctly inferred currency look the same; it gives no per-field signal for the 9-of-10 count.

H3 has no tolerance or rounding rule (paise, CGST+SGST split, rounding-off lines), and no instruction on what to output when the invoice itself doesn't add up: keep printed numbers and fail, or block the row.

H2 fixes date format but not number format (commas, decimals, currency symbols), CSV quoting for supplier names with commas, or whether a header row is included; any of these break an import even when the values are right.

Definition of good says 'import without fixing' but there is no line for 'needs human check' rows, so a correctly flagged bad invoice counts as a failure against the 9/10 decision instead of a success.
The decision doesn't say who checks the 10 rows against the PDFs or how; the model's own scorecard can't be the judge since it marks inferred fields as matching.
prompt_problems: The scorecard only allows Pass or Fail, so when a field isn't on the invoice the model is forced to pick Pass; there is no 'Cannot tell / not on invoice' result, which is the exact failure the graders flagged in 3 of 4 runs.
Hard lines are pasted as 'Pass when Every field matches...' with no instruction on missing or inferred values: no 'leave blank and flag' or 'never infer a value and call it a match'.
'Final output' is free-form, so the CSV row can arrive wrapped in prose or code fences and not be importable; the prompt never says 'output exactly one CSV line, no header, nothing else'.
Step 4 'Fix every Fail' invites the model to change numbers to make H3 pass; it should say fix your own errors, never change the invoice's printed values.

No judge prompt was produced from the eval (discrimination test: no_judge on every case), so the learner has no separate way to check whether a run is good; the self-grade is the only signal and it is lenient.
S2.best_fix_on_final_page: Add a third result to the scorecard, 'Cannot tell', plus one rule above the hard lines: 'If a field is not printed on the invoice, leave it blank or mark it inferred, list it under Why, and mark that check Cannot tell, never Pass. Never change a printed number to make a check pass; if the invoice contradicts itself, Fail and say what to ask the supplier.' This turns the lenient self-grade into an honest import/don't-import signal without changing the learner's questions.

S3.why: The two qualities are well written, with concrete and checkable ends, and the drafts came out usable and on-voice. But the eval has no hard line against inventing facts, which is the main failure in every run. The self-graded 'Meets the bar: Yes' also stands in for a decision only the learner can make, and the judge could not separate weak drafts from good ones.
eval_problems: No Pass/Fail hard lines at all. The obvious one is missing: 'Every fact, number, name and anecdote comes from my notes', and invention was the top problem in all four runs.
The decision ('8 of 10 I'd post as is') and the definition of good ('people would comment') can only be judged by the learner or after posting. Neither quality measures them.

Q2 'Sounds like me' mixes four things: first person, short sentences, one idea, no emojis or hashtags. A draft can score well on some and badly on others, so the 1 to 5 is fuzzy. Runs passed second-person posts and two-idea posts as 5.
'Sounds like me' has no sample of the learner's real posts, so the model is guessing at the voice.
There is no rule for thin notes. The population includes fragmentary meetup notes, and the eval doesn't say whether to stop, ask, or use placeholders.
Q1 rewards a 'claim peers would argue with'. With nothing tying it to the notes, this pushes the model to invent a provocative thesis and put it in the speaker's mouth.
prompt_problems: The page invented a bar ('every quality 4 or more') the learner never set, then labelled it 'Meets the bar', which reads as if the learner's decision were met.
There is no instruction to use only what is in the notes and to mark anything inferred, so the self-check never looks for invented content.
The scorecard has no row for invented or unsupported lines, and none for what only the learner can judge, so self-grades come out 5/5 every time.
'Fix every score under 4, then check again' lets the model grade its own rewrite upward without showing any evidence. The 'Why' column doesn't require quoting the line being scored.
The output allows placeholders but doesn't say a draft with placeholders cannot be 'post as is'.
The 'aim for' line pastes in the definition of good (comments, stopping the scroll), which the model cannot check and which invites hype.
S3.best_fix_on_final_page: Add a fixed source-faithfulness block to every generated prompt. It should say: use only facts, numbers, names and quotes from the input. Where the input is thin, write [ASK ME: ...] instead of inventing. In the scorecard, list every line not directly supported by the notes. Replace 'Meets the bar' with 'Ready for you to judge: Yes/No', where No covers any invented line or placeholder, plus one sentence saying the real test (would you post it as is, do peers comment) is yours to make.

S4.why: The eval's only hard line joins a checkable test (numbers match the source export) to an outcome no LLM can judge (manager approves with no rework), so every run either wrongly failed H1 or could not judge it, and the judges split on good versus hard_fail outputs. The single quality crams numbers, strategy and completeness into one scale and never names the scope (cloud, vendors, the 15% vs 20% target), so a run that dropped GCP and Zendesk still scored itself well.
eval_problems: H1 is two checks in one: 'every number matches the source export' can be tested, but 'managers approve it for the CFO with no rework' is the definition of good, a future human outcome, not a hard line the LLM can check.
H1 starts with 'Yeah, pass when', which is filler that was copied straight into the prompt.
The population is 'the last 10 requests' plus 'a few' from a transcript, so the count is fuzzy. 'If 8 of 10 pass' needs exactly 10 cases.
The decision says what is gained (240 minutes a week) but not what happens if fewer than 8 pass, or who checks the passes.
Q1 covers number accuracy (already in H1), strategy clarity and 'has everything' on one scale, so a deck can be strong on one and weak on another and the score means nothing.
Q1's 5 anchor ('has everything') never says what everything is. No required sections, no scope (which cost lines: cloud, vendors, headcount), no target (15% or 20%).
Nothing covers what to do when the source export or last deck is missing. The tricky runs had to guess whether to leave blanks or ask.
prompt_problems: The page pasted H1 verbatim, giving 'Pass when Yeah, pass when…'. It does not strip filler or a repeated 'pass when'.
The prompt tells the LLM to Pass or Fail a line that needs a future manager approval, and offers no third option, so the runs marked it Fail when the honest answer was 'cannot tell yet'.
The definition of good (manager approval) appears as both the step 2 target and inside H1, and the prompt does not say it is judged by a person after delivery.
Step 5 says to fix every Fail, but an approval Fail cannot be fixed by the LLM, so the loop has no honest exit.
There is no instruction for missing source data (ask, mark [X], or stop). So the runs behaved differently: one asked, others proceeded with placeholders.
The scorecard has no place to list the assumptions or the scope the LLM chose, so the dropped GCP/Zendesk lines never showed up.
S4.best_fix_on_final_page: Before building the prompt, split any hard line that depends on a person's later approval. Keep the checkable half ('every number matches the source export') as the hard line, move the approval half to a 'Judged by you after delivery' row the LLM cannot score, and let each hard line be marked Pass, Fail, or Cannot tell (missing input), with a 'list what you need' line when it is Cannot tell. Also strip filler like 'Yeah, pass when' from the learner's text.

S5.why: Every field is a placeholder ('good', 'correct', 'some tickets', 'bad'/'good'), so the LLM invents its own bar, grades against that, and reports a Pass or 4/5 that no one earned. Seeded hard fails were still caught, but weak-quality outputs were not, and in every run the model said things it could not verify, such as 'our records show' or invented product features, while passing itself.
eval_problems: Definition of good is 'Good replies', which only repeats the task and gives no target.
Decision 'Use AI if it is good' names no threshold, no action and no alternative, for example 'send without review if every hard line passes on 18 of 20 tickets'.
Population 'Some tickets' does not say which ticket types (billing, data loss, angry or threatening), what volume or what share are tricky.
H1 'it is correct' is not checkable: it does not say correct against what (ticket facts, billing records, product policy), so each run made up its own test.
There is no hard line on promises or invented facts (no unverified refunds, no claimed record checks, no made-up features), which is the failure every run actually showed.
Q1 has empty ends ('1 = bad; 5 = good') with no observable description, so the grader cannot tell weak from strong, which is why the weak_quality test failed for both models.
There is only one quality. Tone, clarity of next steps and asking for missing info are not separated.
The eval says nothing about what a human must check or what the reply may not claim without data the LLM lacks (account, billing, policy).
prompt_problems: It pastes the vague text in unchanged ('Aim for this: Good replies', 'Pass when it is correct') and gives no warning that the criteria cannot be checked.
It lets the model grade itself against criteria it has silently rewritten. Nothing tells it to use the learner's words literally or mark 'Cannot check' when it lacks the data.
There is no 'Cannot verify' result in the scorecard, so Pass/Fail forces a false Pass when correctness depends on records the model does not have.

There is no instruction against stating facts beyond the input, such as records, policies or product features, or against promising outcomes. The runs invented 'our records show', a trash folder and refund timing.
Step 5 ('fix every score under 4') pushes the model to inflate its own scores against a scale with no anchors, rather than flag that the scale is empty.
'Meets the bar: Yes' can be reported even when the eval itself is too vague to set a bar, which gives the learner false confidence.
There is no line for listing assumptions or placeholders, or for what a human must confirm before sending.

Q4 Readability depends on a PM's judgement, and the eval gives no concrete test for it, such as no unexplained system or config names
There is no quality or hard line against adding claims beyond the input, such as 'nobody is signed out' or an unsupported cause-and-effect or recommendation
H3 'what changed in one sentence first' was met with line counts and paths, so the eval should say the first sentence describes the change in terms of behaviour, not files
The population lists PR types but not what each input contains (diff, description, link), so runs differ in what the LLM can verify
prompt_problems: The prompt never tells the model to score only against what is in the input, so it claims 'matches the diff' when it saw no diff
'Meets the bar: Yes or No' invites a per-PR verdict, but the learner's decision is 8 of 10 across the population; the prompt does not separate 'this summary passes' from 'the bot can auto-post'
The prompt has no step to list claims not supported by the input before scoring Accuracy, so invented guarantees slip through with 5/5
The prompt does not ask the model to flag which qualities need a human (Readability for a PM), so it scores them with false confidence
The input placeholder does not say what to paste (PR number, URL, description, diff), so H6 and Accuracy fail for input reasons rather than output reasons
Step 5 'fix every score under 4' pushes the model to inflate its own scores rather than admit limits
S6.best_fix_on_final_page: Add one instruction above the scorecard: 'Score only against what is in the input. If you did not see something (the diff, the PR link), say so in Why, cap that score at 3, and mark any check a person must judge as "needs human". Meets the bar is for this one summary; the auto-post decision needs 8 of 10.' Also replace the input placeholder with a short list of what to paste: PR number, PR link, description, diff.

S7.why: The eval's main hard line and its definition of good are both a future human outcome (clearing the interview loop) that no resume can show, so the self-check either passes it dishonestly or fails it misleadingly, and the judges could not reliably tell good outputs from seeded bad ones. The year-band line and the Fit quality are usable, but Fit is written ambiguously enough that runs scored the candidates' resumes instead of the AI's reasoning, so the 'Meets the bar' verdict tells the learner little.
eval_problems: H1 'the candidate clears the interview loop' cannot be checked from a resume at shortlist time; it is the outcome the decision is trying to predict, not a check on the output.
The definition of good is the same unobservable future outcome, so the prompt aims the draft at something it cannot see.
H1 and H2 are written about a candidate, not about the shortlist output, so the checker grades resumes instead of the AI's work.
H2 gives no rule for resumes where backend years are unclear, so runs split between Fail and hold.
Fit's ends do not say whether they rate the AI's reasoning or the candidate's experience, and 5 does not require comparing candidates against each other (e.g. payments work vs an HR portal).
The decision compares against the HM's final picks, but no line checks agreement with the HM's shortlist criteria, which would be the testable proxy.
There is no line on invented facts, yet runs presented guessed system details (latency, idempotency) as facts about a candidate's work.
prompt_problems: The page passes H1 through as 'Pass when the candidate clears the interview loop' with no warning that it cannot be judged from the input, forcing the model to pick between a false Pass and a misleading Fail.
Pass/Fail allows no 'cannot tell' result, so missing information (D's backend years, the future loop result) gets forced into Fail and makes 'Meets the bar: No'.
The prompt never says hard lines and qualities grade the output, so the models scored individual candidates and the 'To make it a 5' fixes pointed at resumes the learner cannot change.
Step 5 says 'fix every Fail', but a Fail caused by the input or by a future event cannot be fixed by redrafting, which invites the model to fudge the check.
The 'Aim for this' line copies an unobservable outcome into the task instructions without turning it into something checkable from the resume.
S7.best_fix_on_final_page: Before building the prompt, flag any hard line that depends on a future event or human outcome (like 'clears the interview loop') and give the learner a one-click rewrite to a line checkable from the input. Also add a 'Cannot tell from the input' result to the scorecard, plus one instruction: 'Every line grades the shortlist and its reasoning, not the candidates; mark a line Cannot tell when the input or a future event decides it, and never count that as Pass.'

S8.why: The two hard lines are checkable, and the runs produced short, mostly accurate replies that staff could send with light edits, so the eval does steer the LLM toward usable output. But nothing grounds the reply in the bakery's real facts or the owner's real voice. Across runs the model guessed dates, promised extras like name-writing on the cake, self-scored Warmth it cannot judge, and declared 'Meets the bar: Yes' from a single reply, so the learner cannot trust the scorecard to tell them when a reply is good.
eval_problems: The definition of good ('lead replies back and books a cake') is an outcome you only see later. It cannot be judged from the reply itself, so nothing in the eval says what makes a reply 'sendable'.

The decision depends on '8 of 10 sendable', but 'sendable' is never defined. There is no hard line for 'only states facts the bakery actually offers' or 'no promises about dates, availability or customisation it hasn't confirmed'. Those were exactly the failures seen (assumed Saturday, invented name-writing, an invented past order).
H1 ('price bataye agar pucha ho') needs a price list to check against, and none was given. The eval also doesn't say what happens when price wasn't asked (Pass or not applicable).
There is no hard line for a clear next step, such as ending with a booking question (flavour, size, date, pickup or delivery). That step is the thing most likely to lead to a booking.

Warmth's 5 anchor, 'like I talk to regulars', refers to a voice the LLM has never seen. Without two or three real example replies, neither the model nor a judge can score it. This is why the weak-quality output was not caught by either judge.
There is only one quality, and its 1 anchor ('robotic') is vague. A polite but generic reply could score 3 to 4, so weak quality slips through.
prompt_problems: 'Aim for this: Lead replies back and books a cake' turns an after-the-fact business outcome into a drafting target. That pushes the model toward confident promises, such as Saturday availability, to close the sale.

There is no slot for the bakery's facts (prices, delivery charge, cutoffs, eggless and customisation options) or for the owner's sample replies. The model either guesses them or relies on whatever happens to appear in the input.
There is no instruction to ask the lead or flag the gap when something is missing or depends on today's date or stock. Instead the model silently guesses.
The scorecard asks the model to grade Warmth against the owner's voice, which it cannot do. The result is unverified 5/5 scores and 'no changes needed'.
'Meets the bar: Yes or No' implies one reply can meet the bar, which conflates a single output with the learner's 8-of-10 decision across the population.
The model is asked to verify its own word count (H2) and miscounted, with no instruction to count explicitly.
Pasting 'Pass when price bataye agar pucha ho' verbatim leaves the not-asked case undefined, so the check is ambiguous.
S8.best_fix_on_final_page: Add a required 'Your bakery's facts' block (prices, delivery, cutoffs, what you can and can't do) and a 'Two or three replies you've actually sent' block above the Input. Add one rule in the task steps: 'Use only these facts; if the answer isn't here or depends on today's date or availability, ask the lead instead of promising.' Then replace 'Meets the bar' with 'Sendable as-is? Yes/No (owner confirms Warmth against the sample replies; this is 1 of your 10)'.
